title: Regions, Availability Zones & Global Infrastructure
summary: The physical and logical geography of a cloud provider, and how it shapes latency, durability, and what actually fails together.

slides.markdown:
A cloud provider's global footprint isn't one giant data center — it's dozens of independent locations, each subdivided again, so that one power outage or fiber cut can't take everything down at once.

Think of it like a country with **states** (regions) made of **neighborhoods** (Availability Zones) on independent power grids, plus small **delivery depots** (edge locations) scattered everywhere for speed.

- Where you place things determines your latency, your durability, and your blast radius when something breaks.

slides.subTitle: The three levels of geography
slides.markdown:
A **region** is a geographic area (e.g. "us-east-1") containing multiple **Availability Zones (AZs)** — physically separate data centers within that region, close enough for low-latency links but far enough apart to have independent power and cooling. **Edge locations** are much smaller, far more numerous points of presence used to cache and serve content close to users, not to run your core workloads.

Regions are for placement and compliance decisions; AZs are for resilience within a region; edge locations are for latency to end users.

slides.subTitle: Independent failure domains
slides.markdown:
An AZ is engineered to be an **independent failure domain**: its own power substation, its own cooling, its own network connection back to the internet backbone. A generator failure or a fiber cut in one AZ shouldn't touch another.

This is why "deploy across multiple AZs" is the single highest-leverage resilience move in cloud architecture — it turns a data-center-level outage from "my app is down" into "a third of my capacity briefly dipped."

Within one region, AZs are wired together by high-bandwidth, low-latency private links, while each keeps its own power and cooling.

![A region containing multiple Availability Zones with inter-AZ links](assets/region-az-layout.svg)

Traffic between AZs in the same region stays fast (sub-ms to low-single-digit ms) and cheap — traffic crossing to another region goes over the public internet or a dedicated backbone and costs noticeably more.

slides.subTitle: Same-AZ, cross-AZ, cross-region
slides.markdown:
| Placement | Latency | Failure protection |
|---|---|---|
| Same AZ | Lowest (sub-ms) | None — one incident can take out both |
| Cross-AZ, same region | Low (low single-digit ms) | Protects against a single AZ failure |
| Cross-region | Higher (tens to 100+ ms) | Protects against a whole-region event |

**How to decide:** keep chatty, latency-sensitive components (app server to cache) in the same AZ pair where possible, spread replicas across AZs for resilience, and only go cross-region when you need protection from a region-wide event or must serve users on another continent.

Region choice is driven by three forces, usually in tension: **data residency** (some regulations require EU customer data to stay in an EU region), **user latency** (pick the region closest to your actual users), and **service availability** (not every provider service ships in every region on day one).

A global product often ends up multi-region not for durability but simply because no single region is close to every user *and* compliant for every jurisdiction at once.

slides.subTitle: What each actually buys you
slides.markdown:
| | Multi-AZ | Multi-region |
|---|---|---|
| Protects against | AZ-level failure (power, cooling, one data center) | Region-wide failure (natural disaster, regional network event) |
| Latency cost | Negligible | Real — cross-region replication lag |
| Complexity | Low — most managed services do it for you | High — you often own the failover logic |

**How to decide:** multi-AZ is close to a default for anything production; multi-region is a deliberate, expensive decision reserved for the workloads whose downtime cost genuinely justifies it.

slides.subTitle: A 3-tier app across AZs
slides.markdown:
Take a standard web/app/database stack: place at least two web-tier instances and two app-tier instances in **different AZs** behind a load balancer, so losing one AZ still leaves capacity serving traffic. For the database, run a primary in one AZ with a synchronous standby in another — if the primary's AZ fails, the standby promotes with no data loss.

This one pattern — spread every tier across at least two AZs — is the baseline every production 3-tier deployment should meet before adding anything fancier.

**Wrong belief:** "My app is multi-AZ, so it's protected from any outage."

**Why it's wrong:** multi-AZ protects against a single data center failing — it does nothing if the whole region has a control-plane incident, a region-wide network event, or a major natural disaster. Several real cloud outages have taken down every AZ in a region at once.

**Correct model:** multi-AZ is your baseline resilience; only multi-region protects against a region-wide event, and you should consciously decide whether that risk is worth the extra cost and complexity.

Edge locations run a small slice of infrastructure — enough to cache content, terminate TLS, and run lightweight edge functions — but they don't host full VMs, databases, or your core compute. There are typically hundreds of edge locations versus a couple dozen regions.

A CDN request often never reaches your region at all: the edge location serves a cached response and only reaches back to origin on a cache miss. That's why CDNs cut latency dramatically without you doing any region-placement work.
